tierWindow.goal: Extend and evaluate searches deeply: run comprehensive, precise searches across the full range of tools, and judge what you find against explicit criteria, defending your decisions.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Evaluation, synthesis and justification; the learner appraises sources, designs a multi-tool strategy, and reasons about coverage and precision.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Open-ended, multi-tool searches where the right coverage is itself a judgement; competing criteria and precision-recall trade-offs weighed.
tierWindow.autonomy: Low scaffolding; the learner designs and defends their own strategy; feedback probes reasoning rather than confirming a single right answer.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner can already search competently: they build keywords and synonyms, run a discovery-service search, and plan from a question. This course assumes that groundwork and develops depth, extending a search across databases and citation trails and evaluating what it returns with rigour. Do not re-teach the basics of what searching is or how to form a first query.

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, evaluating sources with rigour: judging quality against explicit criteria. Second, extending your search: reaching past the discovery service into databases and citation trails. Third, refining for precision: controlling what a search returns and iterating it deliberately. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This advanced course is about the deep end of finding and using sources: judging what you find with rigour, and reaching past the obvious to find what a quick search misses. It assumes you can already build and run a search. By the end you will be able to evaluate sources against explicit criteria, extend a search across databases and citation trails, and refine a search for precision and recall.

At this level, a competent search is not the finish line. The sources you choose, and the ones you discard with reasons, shape the quality of everything you write. Searching well is a scholarly judgement, and it is one your markers and, later, your professional field will expect you to defend.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: evaluate sources against criteria, extend a search past the discovery service, refine a search for precision and recall.

practiceConnection.academic: Finding and using sources well is the engine of independent research. Every literature review, every dissertation, every evidence-based argument you make rests on a search that was wide enough to be fair and sharp enough to be useful, and on sources you judged rather than simply collected. These are the habits that separate competent work from genuinely scholarly work, and they carry straight into research and professional practice.

decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Finding and using sources is no longer about running a search and taking the first page: it is a scholarly judgement you can make and defend. You can evaluate a source against explicit criteria of source type, currency, authority and relevance. You can extend a search past the discovery service into subject databases and along citation trails, backwards and forwards. And you can refine a search for precision and recall, iterating it deliberately. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, these habits are the foundation of independent research. Each literature review you scope, each database you search rather than settle for the first results, each source you weigh and justify, is this craft at work. It is also what research and professional practice reward: the ability to find the evidence that matters, judge it, and stand behind the choices you made.

courseReferences.title: See pages 95 to 112 of Chapter 7, 'Research: Developing Effective Search Strategies', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
